lines.text: Bombay. Nineteen ninety-one.
India has enough foreign currency to pay for just a few weeks of imports.
So the country does the unthinkable.
It sends the nation's gold abroad... as security for a loan.
And it tries to do it in secret.
This is the year India pawned its gold.
Chapter one. The perfect storm.
August, nineteen ninety. Iraq invades Kuwait.
Within weeks, oil prices double.
Over a hundred thousand Indian workers are evacuated from the Gulf. And the money they sent home... dries up.
At home, politics is in turmoil. In November, the V. P. Singh government falls.
Chandra Shekhar becomes Prime Minister, at the head of a minority government.
Ratings agencies downgrade India. Non-resident Indians start pulling out their money.
War abroad. Chaos at home. A perfect storm.
Chapter two. Running on empty.
In August nineteen ninety, India's reserves stand at three point one billion dollars. By January, they are below nine hundred million.
Months later, the Finance Minister will tell Parliament: we have been at the edge of a precipice since December nineteen ninety.
And the reserves keep falling, month after month.
Soon, just two weeks of imports are left.
For the first time ever, India is close to defaulting on its foreign debt.
The country has one big asset left. Gold.
Chapter three. The first gold.
The first gold to go is government gold, seized from smugglers.
In May, twenty tonnes are moved to Union Bank of Switzerland.
Sold, with an option to buy it back.
The deal raises about two hundred million dollars. It buys a little time.
On the twenty-first of May, mid-campaign, Rajiv Gandhi is assassinated.
In June, P. V. Narasimha Rao becomes Prime Minister.
His surprise choice for Finance Minister: the economist, Manmohan Singh.
Chapter four. The airlift.
On the first of July, the rupee is devalued. Two days later... it happens again.
In three days, the rupee loses nearly a fifth of its value.
Now the Reserve Bank turns to its own gold.
Its destination: London.
Under tight security, it's flown out on a chartered cargo plane.
Over two weeks in July, forty-six point nine one tonnes of gold leave Bombay for London.
It goes into the vaults of the Bank of England.
Pledged to the Bank of England and the Bank of Japan...
...for a loan of about four hundred million dollars.
Two central banks. One loan. And India's gold as security.
When the news breaks, the country is stunned.
For many, it feels like a family selling its jewellery.
Chapter five. An idea whose time has come.
Twenty-fourth of July, nineteen ninety-one. Manmohan Singh rises to present his first Budget.
On the same day, industrial licensing is scrapped for all but eighteen industries.
And he ends his speech with a line from Victor Hugo.
No power on earth can stop an idea... whose time has come.
The licence raj begins to crumble.
Quotas and controls start to fall. India opens up to the world.
Chapter six. The return.
By the end of nineteen ninety-one, the loans are repaid, and the pledge is released.
Today, India holds one of the largest foreign exchange reserves in the world.
In twenty twenty-four, the RBI brought one hundred tonnes of its gold home from Britain.
India didn't just survive nineteen ninety-one. It was reborn.
